--- TEXT ---
The phenomenology of genuine aesthetic experience is fundamentally distinct from the mere expression of personal liking, as it inherently involves a claim to intersubjective validity. When an observer encounters a work of profound beauty, the resulting judgment is not experienced as a private, idiosyncratic reaction akin to a preference for a particular flavor of food. Rather, to judge a work as beautiful is to make a claim that extends beyond the self, implicitly calling upon others to share in the same appreciation. This normative dimension is built into the very grammar of aesthetic pronouncements; we do not merely report our internal psychological states by saying that a work pleases us, but instead attribute a value to the work itself, expecting that any similarly situated observer ought to recognize this quality. A purely subjectivist framework is entirely unable to explain this felt demand for agreement, as it reduces all aesthetic judgments to autobiographical reports of pleasure, thereby erasing the distinctively normative weight that characterizes our actual encounters with art.

This claim to validity is not a mere psychological illusion but is actively sustained by the collective practice of aesthetic criticism, which presupposes that evaluations are answerable to considerations beyond individual response. The entire institution of criticism—with its reliance on reasons, formal standards, and the cultivation of taste through education—operates on the assumption that some aesthetic assessments are objectively better-informed, more perceptive, and more coherent than others. When a critic defends an evaluation, they do not simply describe their feelings; they direct our attention to specific, observable features of the artwork, such as its structural harmony, thematic depth, or innovative technique, demonstrating how these elements justify a particular interpretation and valuation. If aesthetic value were nothing more than a projection of subjective preference, the concepts of aesthetic education and the refinement of taste would be meaningless, as there would be no standard against which to measure progress or to distinguish a mature, deeply considered judgment from a superficial one.

Furthermore, any attempt to escape these objective demands through aesthetic relativism inevitably generates a self-defeating logical regress that undermines the position from within. The relativist argues that because all aesthetic judgments are ultimately grounded in subjective preference, no single standard of taste can claim authority over another, meaning that a pluralistic tolerance of all preferences is the only coherent stance. However, this insistence on pluralism and the rejection of dogmatism is itself a value judgment, representing a specific preference for open-mindedness over hierarchical exclusion. If the relativist’s primary assertion is true—that all preferences are merely subjective psychological states with no objective validity—then their own preference for pluralism is likewise nothing more than an arbitrary, subjective whim. To claim that pluralism is the correct or superior approach is to appeal to an objective standard of validity that the relativist’s own theory denies, while to admit that pluralism is merely one arbitrary preference among others is to strip the relativist position of any normative force, reducing it to a hollow assertion that cannot coherently defend itself against dogmatism.
--- END ---
